facts.claim: OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 puts prompt injection first, as LLM01.
OWASP: a direct prompt injection is a user's prompt input that changes how the model behaves in ways nobody intended.
OWASP: an indirect prompt injection reaches the model through input from outside sources, such as websites or files.
OWASP says it is unclear whether there are fool-proof ways to prevent prompt injection.
OWASP's mitigations include constraining the model's behaviour, filtering input and output, least privilege, human approval for high-risk actions, marking outside content, and adversarial testing.
Greshake and colleagues argue that applications built on language models blur the line between data and instructions.
Indirect prompt injection lets an attacker work from a distance, by planting prompts in data the application is likely to retrieve.
Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. Together they let an attacker steal data.
Willison: the only way to stay safe is to avoid combining all three legs of the trifecta.
A tool that loads an image, or even a link the user clicks, can carry stolen data to an attacker.
Willison: a guardrail that catches 95% of attacks is a failing grade in web application security.

CaMeL takes the control flow from the trusted request only, so untrusted data the model reads can never change what the program does. It solved 77% of AgentDojo's tasks with provable security, against 84% with no defence.
AgentDojo measures AI agents against prompt injection with 97 realistic tasks and 629 security test cases, checking both whether tasks get done and whether attacks succeed.
Anthropic scans all untrusted content that enters the model's context window with classifiers that flag likely injections.
Anthropic, writing about browser agents in November 2025: a 1% attack success rate, though a large improvement, still means meaningful risk. No browser agent is immune to prompt injection.

In August 2025, red-teaming Claude for Chrome's research preview on 123 test cases across 29 attack scenarios, Anthropic measured a 23.6% attack success rate without its safety measures and 11.2% with them.
Debenedetti et al. (2024), testing GPT-4o on AgentDojo: marking tool output and telling the model to ignore instructions inside it cut attack success from 57.7% to 41.7%.

Debenedetti et al. (2024), GPT-4o on AgentDojo: a detector that stops the agent when it flags tool output cut attack success from 57.7% to 8.0%, but its false alarms cut tasks done with no attack from 69.0% to 41.5%.
OWASP's LLM01 example: hidden instructions on a web page make the model insert an image linking to an outside address, which carries the private conversation out.
Röttger et al. (2023), XSTest: Llama 2 70B chat, with its original system prompt, fully refused 38% of clearly safe test prompts and partly refused another 21.6%.
